detail.title: Woman Entrepreneurs in Kosovo
detail.abstract:
Woman entrepreneurs in Kosovo

The entrepreneurship has no long history of the activity in Kosovo. This activity has started during the second half of last century, mainly with small businesses.  During the eighties, the private business got a new strength, more rapid in all sectors. The number of businesswoman during this period of time has been very low. This was due to inability for starting a private business as well as due to the lack of sufficient experience in this sector.

During the nineties, the private entrepreneurship, both for man and woman has been brought to minimum due to a inconvenient situation for developing a business. Even the small number of private businessman or businesswoman who was doing business did not have an appropriate legality from the Serbian regime installed in the economy of Kosovo then. A lot of people became jobless as a consequence of massive violent termination of the employment in the social sector by Serbian regime; therefore they were forced to work “illegally”.

The number of businesswoman registered in the government institutions during the nineties was very low, while after the year 2000, they started to work as entrepreneurs in a regular way, in a full compliance with the legislation of the Republic of Kosovo. This number is rapidly increasing as a result of the aid extended from different international organizations as well as different donors, through financial aid or the professional training provided for them. Despite that the profit of businesswoman is rather low, they have still partiallity to create a better life for them and their families, employing an appropriate number of workers, mainly family members and relatives.

title: Using 21st Century Technology To Promote Transparency In Governance
affiliations: Lead City University

detail.title: Using 21st Century Technology To Promote Transparency In Governance
detail.abstract: Transparency in governance has become a pressing need today, as people everywhere are demanding actions that rebuild trust, reduce corruption, and make government truly accountable. This paper looks at how the use of technology; what we now call e-government or digital governance; can answer that call for openness. Transparency, which is simply making public data available and involving citizens in decisions, matters across all arms of government: the legislature, executive, and judiciary. By using digital skills like computer programming, database and software development, cloud computing, cybersecurity, data analytics, artificial intelligence, and even digital communication, we can create systems that open up these processes. Examples such as Latvia’s live-streamed plenary sessions, Brazil’s e-Democracia portal, Ukraine’s open budget sites, and Abu Dhabi’s fully digital court show what is possible when technology is applied well. Yes, challenges like funding shortages, data privacy risks, and skills gaps remain, but these should not stop the shift. Now more than ever, our societies must embrace these tools if we are to restore faith in government, improve governance processes, and secure a future where democracy and accountability are not just ideals but realities.

title: Integrating the Literature: Theory and Evidence from a Reassessment of the Empirical Research on Vertical Integration
affiliations: NERA Economic Consulting, Kelley School of Business, Indiana University and NERA Economic Consulting

detail.title: Integrating the Literature: Theory and Evidence from a Reassessment of the Empirical Research on Vertical Integration

declarations.funderStatement: Computer & Communications Industry Association (CCIA) funded this study. They provided no commentary on the paper.

detail.abstract: This paper reexamines the empirical literature on vertical integration to assess whether, as some commentators have suggested, it suggests that increased antitrust scrutiny of vertical integration is warranted. Following decades of theoretical and empirical consensus suggesting procompetitive welfare effects from vertical integration, more recent reviews of the empirical literature have reached starkly different and contradictory conclusions about its implications for antitrust policy. Thus, we undertake a comprehensive reassessment of the empirical literature using systematic criteria based on welfare outcomes to categorize papers as providing evidence of procompetitive, anticompetitive, or neutral effects of vertical integration and ranking papers based on the strength of their empirical methodology. We find many instances of procompetitive effects, some instances of neutral effects, and few instances of anticompetitive effects. When attention is limited to evidence from the strongest identification strategies, we find only procompetitive or neutral effects, with most papers indicating procompetitive effects. We then turn to two simple theoretical models of vertical integration popular in the economic literature to assess whether economic theory can help explain this pattern of observed results. Consistent with our review, we find that under standard assumptions, the elimination of double marginalization tends to dominate or limit anticompetitive effects. We interpret our results as providing evidence in favor of the efficacy of traditional enforcement patterns and the importance of distinct treatment of vertical versus horizontal mergers by antitrust enforcers.

detail.abstract: This comprehensive review examines the transformative role of Autonomous AI in reshaping organizational structures, decision-making, and operational workflows. With a focus on generative AI's potential, the paper introduces a multi-level framework that spans Infrastructure, Intelligence Augmentation, and Institutional Readiness, synthesizing both theoretical and empirical perspectives. As Autonomous AI continues to redefine enterprise capabilities, from decisionmaking and operational automation to governance and workforce transformation, the article integrates global case studies, academic research, and industry reports to assess both opportunities and risks. The review provides novel insights into the strategic implications of AI adoption, highlighting the challenges organizations face in converting AI pilots into sustained, value-driven solutions. In particular, it emphasizes the "GenAI Divide," a phenomenon where widespread adoption fails to translate into tangible value due to insufficient integration of feedback loops, persistence mechanisms, and workflow compatibility. Addressing this gap, the paper identifies the critical infrastructure, cognitive readiness, and institutional capabilities necessary to bridge the divide and achieve successful AI deployment at scale. Furthermore, it offers actionable policy recommendations, outlines underexplored research areas related to long-term AI system integration, and advocates for inclusive innovation.

detail.abstract: This study presents the development of a novel Quality of Life Index tailored for expat families relocating for the purpose of education. Existing global indices, such as those produced by Numbeo, Mercer, and the World Top 20 Project, provide valuable insights into cost of living, pollution, crime, and educational outcomes, but they often overlook the combined family and relocation needs central to expat decision-making. Using open-source datasets, criteria were defined across two main categories: school quality (including life satisfaction, student–teacher ratio, and immigrant integration) and life quality (including GDP per capita, cost of living, and proportion of foreigners). Data were collated, normalised, and structured in Excel to create a composite ranking of over 60 countries. Despite limitations such as restricted access to comprehensive datasets and the subjectivity of selected criteria, the research produced a comparative tool to assist expat families in evaluating potential destinations. Academically, the project strengthened skills in database research, Excel modelling, and index construction; practically, it provides a structured, family-centred alternative to existing global indices.

title: A Neural Network Based New Approach for the Detection of COVID-19 Diseases
affiliations: University of Tabriz and University of Tabriz

detail.title: A Neural Network Based New Approach for the Detection of COVID-19 Diseases
detail.abstract: Various methods have been proposed to detection of COVID-19 diseases from healthy people. In many of these methods, computed tomography (CT) scans of COVID-19 diseases have been used for classification. In this research, it is assumed that COVID-19 already has affected and damaged the lung tissue of diseases which remains the main pitfall of these methods. Studies show that in many cases, a person infected with COVID-19 has healthy lungs, so there is a need to develop methods to intelligently classify COVID-19 diseases and healthy people based on other clinical information. This research provides a new classification algorithm based on a multilayer artificial neural network (ANN) combined with a jellyfish optimization algorithm to classify healthy and COVID-19 diseases people. To this end, the proposed method uses the jellyfish optimization algorithm to optimize multilayer ANN parameters and select data features. The results show that the proposed algorithm has an accuracy, precision, and sensitivity of 97.44%, 97.41%, and 97.19%, respectively. Based on the results of the present study, the proposed algorithm can be effectively used to detect COVID-19 diseases from healthy ones.

detail.abstract: Public debate often collapses distinct immigration pathways into a single "deportations" scoreboard. This working paper standardizes the core categories used by DHS-Title 8 removals, returns, and (2020-2023) Title 42 expulsions- and demonstrates how shifts in legal pathways, enforcement venues (interior vs. border), and counting rules influence headline numbers. Using the DHS Yearbook of Immigration Statistics, Table 39, as the historical spine and ICE ERO statistics for recent years, we compare 2009-2025 on like-for-like definitions and explain why perceived "toughness" can diverge from formal removal totals. We then extend the systems lens to border device searches to illustrate how institutional rules, rather than rhetoric, determine day-to-day experiences. We conclude with a reporting template and transparency reforms: disaggregated series (removals/returns/expulsions), interior vs. border origin, and standardized footnotes for definitional changes. The goal is comparability, not scorekeeping methods that determine meaning.

title: The Policy Paradox: A Qualitative Analysis of the Public Narrative of New Zealand's Fleeing Driver Policy
affiliations: Victoria University of Wellington - Te Herenga Waka

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author worked for an ambulance organisation at the time the project was started.

declarations.funderStatement: Unfunded.

detail.abstract:
Background: Police pursuits are a significant public health issue globally, with jurisdictions struggling to balance law enforcement with the risk of death and injury. This study analyses the public narrative surrounding New Zealand's dramatic policy cycle on fleeing drivers, which saw a highly restrictive, safety-focused policy reversed, ostensibly due to public pressure.

Methods: We conducted a qualitative document analysis of 28 official reports, policy documents, and media releases from New Zealand Police between 2019 and 2023. The study was intentionally limited to this public-facing narrative. A thematic analysis was performed, and the findings were contextualized with a targeted review of pursuit policies and debates in Australia, the UK, Canada, and the USA.

Findings: The analysis revealed a central "policy paradox"- the 2020 restrictive policy was effective at reducing pursuit-related harm but led to a surge in fleeing incidents. This created a powerful counter-narrative of lawlessness, amplified by media, which made the harm-reduction policy politically untenable. This tension between risk reduction and public perception is a core challenge in other high-income nations, which are also moving towards more restrictive pursuit models despite similar public concerns. 

Interpretation: The New Zealand case study provides a critical, generalisable lesson for global public health and policing: the success of harm-reduction policies in this domain depends not only on their effectiveness but also on managing public perception. Without a proactive strategy to counter narratives of impunity, evidence-based, life-saving policies can fail politically.

title: Purchasing Power: How The U.S. Government Can Use Federal Procurement To Uphold Human Rights
affiliations: Harvard University - Edmond J. Safra Center for Ethics

detail.title: Purchasing Power: How The U.S. Government Can Use Federal Procurement To Uphold Human Rights
detail.abstract:
Workers in countries around the world endure serious human and labor rights violations as they work to make goods for the United States federal government.

In Bangladesh, employees at Manta Apparels, which made uniforms for the General Services Administration (GSA), reported regular beatings and chained fire exits. Children made up a third of the workforce at another Bangladeshi factory manufacturing U.S. Marine Corps shirts to be sold in U.S. military stores.  Workers there reported violence by managers if production quotas were missed and the lack of a functioning alarm system despite past fires.  In Thailand, employees making clothing sold by the Smithsonian Institution, an arm of the U.S. government, reported illegal wage confiscation, physical harassment, and constant surveillance with cameras mounted even in bathrooms. In Cambodia, clothes sold by the U.S. Army and Air Force were being made by workers as young as 15, and some reported being told to hide from inspectors. One worker told The New York Times, “Sometimes people soil themselves at their sewing machines,” because bathroom use is restricted. These are examples of a much larger problem: U.S. federal procurement relies on global supply chains that are often rife with serious human and labor rights violations.

detail.abstract: This study examined the relationship between pre-qualification and procurement efficiency in Rivers State Government ministries. Pre-qualifications were conceptualized as the independent variable, while value for money and public accountability served as measures of procurement efficiency. Two research questions guided the study, which adopted a cross-sectional survey design. The population comprised procurement officers across all 26 ministries in the Rivers State Government ministries. Given the manageable size of the population, a census approach was utilized. Instrument reliability was confirmed using Cronbach's Alpha, with all items scoring above 0.70. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, and two hypotheses were tested using Spearman's Rank Order Correlation at a 95% confidence level and a 0.05 significance threshold. Findings revealed a significant positive relationship between pre-qualification and procurement efficiency within the ministries. The study concludes that adopting pre-qualification requirement in public procurement processes enhances transparency, reduces costs, and improves efficiency. It is recommended that stringent procurement policies be implemented to encourage pre-qualification which will foster efficient procurement practices and properly evaluate the tenders from vendors in order to ascertain the most suitable in terms of technical suitability across all ministries.

title: Reality Check: How to Protect Human Rights in the 3D Immersive Web
affiliations: University of Chicago - Law School

detail.title: Reality Check: How to Protect Human Rights in the 3D Immersive Web
detail.abstract:
The “metaverse,” “extended reality” (XR), and “spatial computing” are all terms that describe what is expected to become the next iteration of the Internet: a sprawling collection of online spaces and applications offering digital content to users in three-dimensional, immersive form. 

Instead of interacting with digital content via two-dimensional images and text on flat screens, consumers will be able to carry out everyday activities—from schooling to work to shopping—in environments that feature 3D computer-rendered objects, places, and people. 

The advent of XR platforms could be as important as the rise of the Internet in the 1990s in terms of its far-reaching, if uncertain, potential to transform daily life. Some claims about the 3D immersive web—what precisely it will look like, who will own it, how much economic value it will yield, and when it will mature —are largely speculative. But other aspects of the new medium are already discernible and raise urgent policy questions. 

This report examines two of the most pressing issues related to the mass adoption of immersive technologies: First, there is the potential erosion of privacy, including mental privacy. XR devices and systems require the processing of users’ bodily data and spatial surroundings. When aggregated and analyzed over time, this data can reveal highly sensitive information about individuals, including their physical and mental states—information that could be exploited for commercial or political gain. The second issue is the proliferation of harmful behavior in virtual environments, including sexual harassment and abuse of children. Experiences in virtual reality often are perceived by users as real and can result in deep and lasting psychological harm. Yet the tools and systems to ensure safety in XR are underdeveloped.

affiliations: Compassion AI, LLC and Temple University - Department of Finance

detail.title: From Analyst Forecasts to the Q-Theory of Corporate Investments: A Novel Methodology for Directly Estimating WACC

publicationDetails.detailsText: Fox School of Business Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Fox School of Business, Temple University Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel methodology for estimating the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) from discounted cash flow models based on analyst forecasts of operating profits. Unlike traditional methods, our approach incorporates forward-looking expectations and directly estimates WACC without the need to individually estimate costs of equity and debt. Cross-sectionally, our methodology assigns higher costs of capital to riskier industries, and our estimated WACC is positively related to volatility, market, SMB, and HML betas, and negatively related to market cap, leverage, debt maturity, and tax rates. Consistent with Q-theory, cross-sectional regressions reveal a significant negative relationship between WACC and future investments. We further find that the underperformance of high-investment firms varies with their cost of capital, offering new insights into investment behavior and challenging traditional risk explanations. In the time series, the aggregate WACC varies considerably across economic cycles and is negatively related to future investment, though this relationship weakens in the presence of the Term Spread, which itself is negatively related to future investment. Our intuitive methodology provides corporate managers a straightforward means of estimating the cost of capital for their investment decisions, while offering researchers a more reliable measure of firm-wide cost of capital.

title: Unpacking the U-shape in mental well-being: The role of unemployment and disability∗
affiliations: USC Center for Economic and Social Research, affiliation not provided to SSRN and VU University Amsterdam

detail.title: Unpacking the U-shape in mental well-being: The role of unemployment and disability∗

publicationDetails.detailsText: LABECO-D-25-00486

detail.abstract: A growing literature reports a U-shape in mental well-being over the life-cycle, with mental health dipping during prime working ages. What is behind the U-shape remains a mystery. However, the U-shape literature has, so far, considered ceteris paribus  population averages. Using Dutch survey data, we uncover a cross-sectional U-shape for unemployed and disabled men and women, but not by educational attainment, household income, or marital status. Exploiting the longitudinal dimension of the survey, we find that the left-hand side of the U-shape for the unemployed and disabled can potentially be attributed to composition effects. However, unemployed and disabled men and women experience significantly larger mental-health improvements with age than do employed individuals in the second half of working life (the right-hand side of the U-shape). Thus, composition effects (left-hand side) and the age pattern of mental wellbeing for the unemployed and disabled (right-hand side) can potentially explain the U-shape. We demonstrate that mental well-being improvements with age are especially robust for unemployed and disabled men, and generally also hold for four other measures of well-being and in other countries and institutional settings, using three health and retirement surveys covering continental Europe, the United States and the United Kingdom.

detail.abstract: This paper extends Leigh Van Valen's Red Queen Hypothesis (1973) into the realm of business ecology. Building on the Law of Constant Extinction, I propose a framework where organizations, like species, must continuously co-evolve within ecosystems shaped by disruption and interdependence. Drawing from over 25 years of executive practice across global organizations and diverse industries, combined with my academic background as an INSEAD GEMBA and AMP graduate and a Harvard-certified educator, I introduce three laws-Adapt, Evolve, Expand-and a Growth Formula that integrates leadership as the multiplier of sustainable relevance. Unlike static strategy models that assume sustainable competitive advantage, this paper argues that in co-evolutionary markets, advantage is inherently transient. Competitive dynamics are often zero-sum, but long-term survival requires transcending this trap through expansion and ecosystem creation. By bridging Van Valen's biological insight with organizational studies, this work contributes a dynamic model for understanding why firms and nations thrive or decline, offering a roadmap for both scholars and practitioners navigating turbulent environments.

detail.abstract: Many individuals experiencing mental health challenges do not seek professional help due to various barriers. One particularly important yet often overlooked factor is stigma concerns, i.e., the fear of judgment. Digital technologies o!er new avenues to mitigate stigma concerns in mental health support. In particular, telehealth and large language model (LLM)-based conversational AI can provide patients with access to mental health services without exposure to onlookers. Yet, it is unclear whether patients value these solutions, given concerns about data privacy. Accordingly, we conducted an online experiment with more than 1,000 participants who reported mental health challenges. We asked participants to evaluate their willingness to engage with advertised mental health services, randomizing service bundles to include di!erent combinations of o"ine appointments, telehealth, and LLM-based conversational AI tools incorporating alternative data privacy assurances. Our results demonstrate that including telehealth and conversational AI increases participants' willingness to engage, particularly when they hold stigma concerns. However, participants' willingness to engage with conversational AI under di!erent privacy guarantees varies markedly depending on stigma concerns. Those with reduced stigma concerns are sensitive to privacy guarantees, whereas those with heightened stigma are relatively insensitive. Our findings highlight the potential of telehealth and conversational AI to increase engagement with mental health services while underscoring the need for nuanced privacy policies to address the tension between stigma and privacy concerns across patient populations.

title: How Generative AI Reshapes Management Education: From Algorithmic Threats to Structured Social Learning

detail.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents an existential challenge to management education, potentially undermining the fundamental processes through which learners develop the knowledge, skills, and practical wisdom essential for organizational leadership. We theorize three distinct mechanisms through which GenAI threatens management learning: algorithmic short-circuiting of conceptual knowledge, whereby learners bypass the cognitive struggle necessary for deep understanding; algorithmic displacement of skills, wherein both technical competencies and social capabilities atrophy through substitution; and algorithmic decontextualization of practical wisdom, which removes judgment from its social, historical, and imaginative contexts. Drawing on established learning theory and our analysis of management education's unique challenges, we develop the concept of Structured Social Learning (SSL) as a pedagogical response that deliberately orchestrates protective and generative practices across these knowledge domains. Through six theoretical propositions, we specify how learning environments must be reconceptualized when algorithmic supports fundamentally alter the conditions of management learning and education. Our framework reveals that the challenge facing business schools is not whether to integrate GenAI but how to orchestrate productive tensions between efficiency and depth, agency and dependency, thereby preserving the essential inefficiencies through which management capability develops in an algorithmic age.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) governance has largely been defined by principles, voluntary frameworks, and point-in-time certifications. While these approaches provide important starting points, they lack enforceability and continuous accountability. With the acceleration of adaptive machine learning systems and the adoption of regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act and ISO/IEC 42001, governance requires mechanisms that operate at the same scale and dynamics as the systems they regulate.

This paper introduces the AIGN OS Trust Infrastructure, the first integrated enforcement model for responsible AI governance. It combines three mechanisms that have so far been discussed only in isolation:

  1. Trust Labels – visible signals of governance maturity and compliance.

  2. Certification Pathways – continuous, risk-based assurance cycles aligned with global standards.

  3. Licensing Logic – embedding governance obligations into contractual and commercial structures.

Together, these mechanisms transform governance from static documentation into a continuous, certifiable, and market-operational system. The model is illustrated through case applications in education (Trust Label deployment in Seoul), enterprise (ERP and supply chain integration), and government (readiness benchmarking and certification).

The contribution of this work is twofold: (1) it closes the trust gap between high-level governance principles and enforceable practice, and (2) it establishes scientific prior art for certification, licensing, and trust infrastructures in AI governance. By doing so, it offers regulators, enterprises, and standardization bodies a blueprint for embedding accountability, comparability, and trust directly into AI markets.

publicationDetails.detailsText: LEAQUA-D-25-00739

detail.abstract: The study examines the effectiveness of United States Coast Guard leadership training in mid-level leaders for e-leadership during crises, using the COVID-19 pandemic as a catalyst. The pandemic-induced shift to remote work highlighted potential gaps in how USCG training equips leaders to navigate e-leadership challenges, particularly in supporting essential constructs like communication, emotional intelligence, trust, and decision-making in digitally mediated environments. This qualitative exploratory research aimed to understand the influence of USCG training on leaders’ abilities to address these challenges. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 28 USCG mid-level leaders and analyzed using thematic analysis. Key findings reveal that formal USCG training had a limited direct impact on e-leadership preparedness. Leaders predominantly relied on on-the-job training, mentorship, and personal initiative, with human-centric leadership emerging as critical. Deficiencies in specific e-leadership modules, digital literacy, and infrastructure were also identified. The study offers theoretical insights for e-leadership in military contexts. It provides practical recommendations for the USCG, including curriculum reform and infrastructure improvements, to enhance leadership development for future high-stakes scenarios.

title: Inferring Intent from AI-Mediated Interactions: A Comparison of LLMs vs. Traditional Graph Methods
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland - Department of Marketing and University of Maryland, Robert H. Smith School of Business

detail.title: Inferring Intent from AI-Mediated Interactions: A Comparison of LLMs vs. Traditional Graph Methods
detail.abstract: This study examines and compares the ability of traditional graph methods and LLMs in inferring intent from consumer interactions with their AI assistants. Specifically, we focus on purchase intent. We compare inferred purchase intent using a graph-based method versus an LLM-based method to those provided by human annotators and market metrics such as CPC. Our findings suggest that both graph-and LLM-based methods can predict purchase intent, but key differences exist. Our analyses demonstrate the value of both LLMs and traditional graph-based methods. LLMs capture the value of verbs while the graph is better able to capture the value of nouns that provide important contextual information. Overall, we show that graph-based methods and LLM-based methods are not necessarily substitutes but rather complements. The ability to infer consumer intent, specifically purchase intent, has implications for AI orchestration and advertising strategies.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is disrupting traditional assumptions about law students’ authorship of their written assignments.  Faculty are concerned about their ability to tell whether students are writing their own papers or simply using AI tools like ChatGPT.  This article offers practical strategies for addressing this problem, focusing on teaching and grading practices that promote transparency, accountability, and learning.

It recommends that faculty require students to include AI use certification cover sheets with their papers, disclosing whether and how they used AI tools during the writing process.  The article also explains how faculty can shift from purely summative to use more formative assessments, which provide insight into students’ thinking and help them improve their analysis and writing.  It suggests that faculty assign shorter, staged tasks and require students to use AI for some of them.  Faculty can review AI chat transcripts to better understand student thinking and provide well-focused feedback.

Rather than trying to determine whether students used AI tools, these approaches give faculty better methods to assess authorship and promote learning.  They also help faculty adapt their teaching practices to the realities of AI-influenced writing.  The article includes sample language for syllabi, grading rubrics, and assignment design.

detail.abstract: In recent years, generative AI has emerged as a transformative and disruptive force, with the potential to reshape professional practices, resulting in the need to master new skills, such as, for example, prompt engineering. This study specifically explores how four leading generative AI tools-ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and Perplexity address key ethical principles in software engineering, focusing on bias, integrity, and fairness. We propose a novel framework for evaluating ethical testing by combining prompt engineering techniques with expert input. The results show that precise, context-rich prompts significantly improve AI outputs, particularly in code-based ethics testing. Perplexity demonstrated the most comprehensive and actionable responses, followed by Copilot, with ChatGPT offering moderate insights and Gemini providing minimal depth. The research also highlights that prompt engineering is a non-intuitive skill for most users, reinforcing the need for clearer guidelines and structured interaction. Ultimately, the study shows that ethical implementation in generative code can be improved through early learning, expert framing, and effective prompt design.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Axiom Engine, a novel philosophical and operational framework designed to address systemic decay in complex societies. The framework posits that by institutionalizing a fractal, self-correcting architecture based on the core pillars of Truth, Wisdom, and Humanity, systems from the individual to the global level can achieve anti-fragility—the capacity to gain strength from disorder. We first detail the philosophical architecture, which models ethical space as a tetrahedral field. We then describe its operational engine, a synthesis of cybernetic feedback loops and second-order observation. Subsequently, we demonstrate the framework's fractal scalability through proposed redesigns of personal ethics, the U.S. Constitution, the UN Charter, and a solution for the AI alignment problem. The paper argues that the Axiom Engine offers a coherent, scalable, and robust alternative to static governance models, providing a generative protocol for navigating 21st-century complexity.

detail.abstract: The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), applicable from 17 January 2025, redefines how financial institutions must address operational risk, shifting the emphasis from procedural compliance to demonstrable resilience. This paper develops the Regulatory-Technical Translation Framework (RTTF), a conceptual model that maps DORA's legal requirements into implementable technical practices for cloud-native environments. The contribution is primarily theoretical, drawing on compliance theory, organisational resilience research, and technology adoption literature to articulate how DevOps and security teams might embed regulatory obligations into the software development lifecycle, Infrastructure as Code (IaC), and observability frameworks. Methodologically, the study is based on structured documentary analysis of regulatory texts and technical standards, from which implementation patterns are derived for different institutional contexts. While the RTTF is not yet validated empirically, it fills a gap in literature that has not systematically addressed how principles-based regulations translate into technical architectures. The paper contributes to literature on regulatorytechnical convergence by offering a theoretically grounded framework for financial services. This foundation enables both future empirical validation and practical experimentation in industry settings.

detail.abstract:
For nearly a century, Abraham Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs shoo served as the fundamental model for human motivation. However, its linear, hierarchical structure fails to capture the Systeme complexity of today's real-world systems, were individuals and organizations often Pursuit higher-level needs despite fundamental deficits.

This paper present Maslow's Fractal™ (Maslow^F™ or MaslowF™ or simply MaslowF™), a new theoretical and operational framework that translates this concept into a rigorous diagnostic tool. The fundamental tenet of the framework is that each of Maslow's five levels is not a monolithic stage, but rather contains a complete Maslowian hierarchy in itself. This fractal nature transforms the classical pyramid into a dynamic diagnostic map: a 25-stringed harp, where each thong represents a distinct sub-need.

I present how this new perspective provides a granular tool for identifying the precise point of failure, the "dissonant chord", in any complex adaptive system, be it an individual, a team, a corporation or organization, a country or alliance, a process or procedure, or even an Artificial Intelligence.

This paper argues that this fractal model provides a more accurate description of motivational dynamics and proposes a universal and actionable guide. It is not an algorithm that provides simple answers, but a fine-tuned instrument, a "25-stringed harp", that allows a skilled analyst to listen to dissonance and guides any complex system towards harmony
and a deep understanding of its own Systeme health.

detail.abstract: The growing adoption of industrial machines in consumer contexts demands efficient predictive maintenance to reduce downtime and material loss. This study investigates anomaly detection for predictive maintenance of 3D printers leveraging real-time sensor data and unsupervised machine learning. A One-Class Support Vector Machine (SVM) is trained on nominal operational sensor readings to define a baseline for expected performance. Subsequently, an anomalous dataset is introduced to assess the model’s capability to identify deviations signaling mechanical failures or functional irregularities. Sensor metrics, such as vibration and temperature, act as primary markers for anomaly detection. The model’s performance is evaluated using a confusion matrix and classification metrics. Initial results reveal challenges in distinguishing anomalies due to parameter settings and dataset structure. Further improvement will focus on refining the anomaly simulation and fine-tuning hyperparameters to enhance sensitivity. This research advances real-time anomaly detection for additive manufacturing, optimizing 3D printing operations and potentially benefiting other technical domains.

title: LLM-Driven Automated Test Case Generation: A Multi-Modal Context-Aware Framework with Formal Quality Guarantees

detail.title: LLM-Driven Automated Test Case Generation: A Multi-Modal Context-Aware Framework with Formal Quality Guarantees
detail.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into software testing represents a paradigm shift in automated quality assurance. This paper presents TESTFORGE, a novel multimodal context-aware framework that leverages the code understanding capabilities of LLMs to generate comprehensive test cases with formal quality guarantees. Our methodology combines static code analysis, dynamic execution profiling, and LLM-powered semantic understanding through a mathematically grounded attention mechanism to produce contextually relevant test scenarios. We introduce novel algorithms for test completeness analysis and provide theoretical bounds on coverage guarantees. Our comprehensive evaluation on 847 opensource projects across five programming languages demonstrates statistically significant improvements: 47.3% increase in branch coverage (p ¡ 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.42), 52.1% improvement in mutation score (p ¡ 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.67), and 39.7% reduction in manual testing effort compared to stateof-the-art automated testing tools. The framework successfully identifies 73.2% more critical defects than baseline approaches, with generated tests exhibiting superior maintainability scores (average cyclomatic complexity of 2.3 vs. 4.7 for human-written tests). Our reproducible experimental artifacts and formal proofs are available for community validation.

detail.abstract: This study examined how social media influencers (SMIs) shape the purchasing behavior of Filipino Generation Z consumers, with a focus on how influencer attributes foster parasocial relationships (PSRs) that drive online shopping. Drawing on Social Media Marketing Theory, Parasocial Interaction Theory, Source Credibility Theory, the Source Attractiveness Model, and Social Proof Theory, this study employed a quantitative-descriptive design using surveys from 380 Gen Z respondents in San Fernando, La Union. Data were analyzed through descriptive statistics, the Mann-Whitney U test, and Spearman’s rho correlation.Results showed that nano-influencers (0–10,000 followers) were most effective in building trust and emotional connection, strengthening PSRs, and influencing purchase intent. Attributes such as authenticity, content style, perceived fit, and popularity were key drivers of engagement, with gender differences observed in PSR strength (higher among females) but not in overall purchasing behavior.The study concludes that relatable and emotionally resonant influencers play a central role in Gen Z’s purchasing decisions. It recommends that brands prioritize collaborations with credible nano-influencers to build long-term trust and loyalty. By situating findings within the Philippine and Southeast Asian context, the research contributes to the literature on influencer marketing while offering practical insights for digital strategies in the post-pandemic economy.

detail.title: Energy-Efficient 5G IoT Architectures: Designing Low-Power 5G IoT Networks to Support Sustainable Smart City Applications
detail.abstract: As the world demand for Internet of Things (IoT) devices increases, the integration of 5G networks is pivotal to making sustainable smart city applications a reality. However, the increasing energy consumption of 5G networks poses severe challenges to achieving sustainability goals. This paper addresses energy-efficient 5G IoT network architectures based on low-power design that can support the heterogeneous and growing demands of smart cities. We examine the interaction between 5G technologies, IoT devices, and energy efficiency, identifying major strategies such as network slicing, edge computing, and low-power design principles for the infrastructure and devices. The paper also examines emerging methods such as energy harvesting, LPWANs, and optimization algorithms to reduce energy consumption with high performance and reliability in 5G-enabled IoT applications. The proposed energy-efficient architectures aim to support smart city use cases such as smart grids, autonomous vehicles, smart traffic management, green environment monitoring, and public safety networks that require high data rates, ultra-low latency, and minimum power consumption. Through the assistance of features like mMTC and URLLC capabilities, we identify how 5G can fulfill challenging requirements of diversified IoT applications and reduce energy costs. Moreover, we emphasize the role of dynamic spectrum management, adaptive power control, and new communication protocols that facilitate power consumption reduction in 5G network infrastructure. This research provides valuable insights into the design of sustainable 5G IoT systems that are capable of fulfilling the performance requirements of modern urban infrastructure without compromising environmental goals. By developing energy-aware architectures that combine cutting-edge 5G technologies with IoT-optimized optimizations, this study supports the realization of energy-aware, scalable, and sustainable smart city solutions that balance technological advancement with environmental responsibility in the face of rapid urbanization.

title: Who Moderates the Social Media Giants? A Call to End Outsourcing
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: Who Moderates the Social Media Giants? A Call to End Outsourcing
detail.abstract:
Content moderation—the process of deciding what stays online and what gets taken down— is an indispensable aspect of the social media industry. Without it, online platforms would be inundated not just by spam, but by personal bullying, neo-Nazi screeds, terrorist beheadings, and child sexual abuse. 


Despite the centrality of content moderation, however, major social media companies have marginalized the people who do this work, outsourcing the vast majority of it to third-party vendors. A close look at this situation reveals three main problems: 


— In some parts of the world distant from Silicon Valley, the marginalization of content moderation has led to social media companies paying inadequate attention to how their platforms have been misused to stoke ethnic and religious violence. This has occurred in places ranging from Myanmar to Ethiopia. Facebook, for example, has expanded into far-flung markets, seeking to boost its user-growth numbers, without having sufficient moderators in place who understand local languages and cultures.


— The peripheral status of moderators undercuts their receiving adequate counseling and medical care for the psychological side effects of repeated exposure to toxic online content. Watching the worst social media has to offer leaves many moderators emotionally debilitated. Too often, they don’t get the support or benefits they need and deserve. 


— The frequently chaotic outsourced environments in which moderators work impinge on their decisionmaking. Disputes with quality-control reviewers consume time and attention and contribute to a rancorous atmosphere. Outsourcing has become a common aspect of the globalized economy. Examples include customer-help centers in the Philippines, digital device factories in China, and clothing-production facilities in Bangladesh. 


Outsourcing is not inherently detrimental—if workers are paid fairly and treated humanely. A central question raised by outsourcing, in whatever industry it occurs, is whether it leads to worker exploitation. In social media, there’s an additional concern about whether outsourcing jeopardizes optimal performance of a critical function.

detail.abstract: The interplay between private provision and equitable access to higher education in Ghana presents a critical paradox: while private institutions are poised to expand educational opportunities and ease pressure on overstretched public universities, their declining enrolment and systemic marginalisation reinforce existing socioeconomic disparities. This paper explores the structural barriers impeding the growth and contribution of Private Higher Education Institutions (PHEIs) to Ghana's national development agenda. Using a qualitative design supported by descriptive statistics and thematic analysis, the study draws on literature, regulatory reviews, institutional documents, and key informant interviews with senior administrators of Ghanaian private universities and primarily from lived experiences of Accra Metropolitan University. The findings reveal that charter delays, rigid affiliation requirements, funding constraints, and policy-induced distortions such as the public perception surrounding the recently announced Free First Year Tuition policy are significantly crowding out private providers. Although the policy has not yet been implemented, widespread state messaging has already begun shifting enrolment preferences and reinforcing affordability narratives favouring public institutions. Ghana's tertiary Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) stood at 21.99 percent in 2023, well below the global average of 40.35 percent. Public universities absorbed 89 percent of enrolments, while the share for private universities dropped to 11 percent, down from 20 percent in 2012. This trend raises critical questions about sustainability, inclusivity, and the strategic role of private providers, especially in reaching underserved and non-traditional learners. Through the lenses of public good theory and coercive isomorphism, the paper argues that Ghana must reframe private provision not as a secondary commercial tier but as a strategic pillar for achieving national equity and inclusion. It recommends differentiated accreditation standards, expanded access to funding, strengthened public-private partnerships, and a transition to outcome-based quality assurance. Without targeted structural reforms, private universities will remain institutionally disadvantaged and Ghana's broader goals for inclusive higher education will remain unrealised.

title: Interview Rounds and Inequality: A Probabilistic Model of Bias Amplification in Sequential Hiring
affiliations: SBS Swiss Business School, Swiss Business School (SBS) and Swiss Business School (SBS) - Department of Management

detail.title: Interview Rounds and Inequality: A Probabilistic Model of Bias Amplification in Sequential Hiring
detail.abstract: Multi-stage interviews are intended to improve hiring accuracy but can unintentionally amplify inequality. We propose the Probabilistic Bias Amplification Model (PBAM), which treats each interview round as shaped by two forces: a neutral (performance-based chance of advancing) and a systematic tilt (bias multiplier) that helps or harms particular groups. Across several rounds, even small tilts at each stage accumulate into significant gaps in who ultimately gets hired-gaps that can remain hidden when stages are assessed in isolation. PBAM integrates insights from signaling theory, procedural justice, and cumulative disadvantage, extending research on structured versus unstructured interviews and pipeline-aware fairness. We offer testable propositions that can be evaluated with Applicant Tracking System data and standard statistical audits of stage-by-stage "survival" rates. Practically, we recommend streamlining excessive rounds, structuring high-discretion stages, and auditing for both penalties (systematic headwinds) and favoritism (systematic tailwinds). By shifting fairness from perception to measurable progression, PBAM provides an actionable basis for diagnosing and reducing bias in human-and AI-mediated recruitment.

detail.title: A Dynamic Model of Authority in Organizations

declarations.funderStatement: the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG) through the Research Project Training Group (RTG 2865)—Coping with Uncertainty in Dynamic Economics (CUDE)

detail.abstract: In our principal-agent model, the principal can repeatedly delegate authority to an agent with uncertain preferences or take the decisions himself. The principal learns the state at the end of each period and then updates his belief about the agent's bias based on the decision implemented if he delegated authority. We demonstrate that equilibria are characterized by an "imitation" interval of agent types (biases) who mimic less biased types in order to be retained. Interestingly, the principal generally benefits from the agent's imitation compared to a benchmark. Furthermore, comparative statics reveal that, surprisingly, the principal may be worse off with better information. Finally, an extension to finitely many periods shows that the imitation interval gradually shifts, such that agent types within the interval imitate less biased types.

title: Made in Ethiopia: Challenges in the Garment Industry’s New Frontier
affiliations: Geneva Center for Business and Human Rights and New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: Made in Ethiopia: Challenges in the Garment Industry’s New Frontier
detail.abstract:
In recent years, Ethiopia has launched a bold economic and social experiment by inviting the global garment industry to set up shop in the East African country. Drawn by newly built industrial parks and a range of financial incentives, manufacturers for some of the world’s best-known brands—among them, H&M and PVH (Calvin Klein, Izod, Tommy Hilfiger)—employ tens of thousands of Ethiopian workers in a nascent sector the government predicts will one day have billions of dollars in sales. 

This report provides a close look at the flagship Hawassa Industrial Park, a vast and still only partly filled facility which currently employs 25,000 workers about 140 miles south of the capital of Addis Ababa.

For all of its potential, the apparel industry in Ethiopia has already encountered difficulties. The government’s eagerness to attract foreign investment led it to promote the lowest base wage in any garment-producing country—now set at the equivalent of $26 a month. On that amount, workers, most of them young women from poor farming families, cannot afford decent housing, food, and transportation. Even when factory owners provide additional modest payments for regular attendance and meals, workers struggle to get by. It’s common for young women to live four-to-a-room, without indoor plumbing.

Given relatively little training, restive employees have protested by stopping work or quitting altogether. Productivity in the Hawassa factories typically is low, while worker disillusionment and attrition are high.

Ethiopian politics are unexpectedly disrupting factory operations. Prime Minister Dr. Abiy Ahmed, chosen in April 2018 by Ethiopia’s long-time ruling party, has freed political prisoners and made peace with neighboring Eritrea. But the easing of repression has inadvertently unleashed previously bottled-up ethnic animosity. In Hawassa, local militancy has become entwined with labor issues, resulting in short strikes at individual factories and occasional park-wide closings.

title: Disinformation and the 2020 Election: How the Social Media Industry Should Prepare
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: Disinformation and the 2020 Election: How the Social Media Industry Should Prepare
detail.abstract:
This report assesses some of the forms and sources of disinformation likely to play a role during the presidential election campaign in 2020. While midterm Election Day in November 2018 did not feature much Russian interference, there is no guarantee that Russia, and possibly other U.S. antagonists, will refrain from digital meddling in the more consequential 2020 contest. What’s more, in terms of sheer volume, domestically generated disinformation now exceeds malign content from foreign sources and will almost certainly be a factor in the next election.

The report explores these risks and analyzes what the major social media companies—Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube (owned by Google)—have done to harden their defenses against disinformation. We also offer recommendations of additional steps the companies need to take to prepare for the almost-certain assault in 2020.

By “disinformation,” we mean a relatively broad category of false or misleading text or imagery which is intentionally or recklessly spread to deceive, propagandize, promote discord, or make money via “clickbait” schemes. For the sake of variety, we sometimes refer to “false content” or “false information.” 

We also refer to a narrower category of disinformation—“provably false content”— which we urge the social media companies to remove. To illustrate, consider these hypothetical examples: An article headlined, “The Sandy Hook Massacre Was Staged,” can be proven definitively untrue and ought to be deleted for that reason. By contrast, a story headlined, “Journalists Really Are the Enemy of the People,” may be unsubstantiated and misleading, but it isn’t provably false.

This report doesn’t cover cyberattacks — remote intrusions into computer networks, such as the Russian hack-and-release of Democratic email in 2016. Cyberattacks on campaigns and state voting systems are a distinct danger in 2020, but they are beyond the scope of this report. Also beyond the scope are the privacy and disclosure issues that led Facebook to agree in July 2019 to pay $5.1 billion in settlements to the federal government and to submit to new types of oversight.

detail.title: The Health Impact of Policy Changes on Fleeing Driver Events in New Zealand: An Interrupted Time Series Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author worked for an ambulance organisation at the time the project was initiated.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This work was undertaken on publicly available data which did not involve human participants. However, as part of an overarching program of work related to transport and police-related policy, HDEC approval was obtained from the Victoria University of Wellington Human Research Ethics Committee-2025/HE040619 - Road, Traffic and Policing: Policy-Related Health and Social Outcomes
declarations.funderStatement: Nil.

detail.abstract:
Background: In late 2020, New Zealand Police implemented a restrictive pursuit policy to reduce harm from fleeing driver events, a policy that was subsequently revised in May 2023 to allow for more officer discretion. This study quantitatively evaluates the impact of these two major policy changes on pursuits, crashes, and related health outcomes.

Methods: A quasi-experimental interrupted time series analysis (ITSA) was conducted on monthly data from January 2017 to March 2025. The primary outcome was the number of Crashes resulting from fleeing driver events. Secondary outcomes included Incidents, Pursuits, Deaths, and Serious Injuries. Segmented regression models, including a final interaction model for Crashes, were used to assess the impact of the December 2020 and May 2023 policy interventions. A comprehensive suite of sensitivity analyses and a formal Granger causality test were conducted to ensure the robustness of the findings.

Results: The 2020 restrictive policy was associated with a significant and immediate level reduction in Crashes (-19.04, p < .001). However, the May 2023 revision was associated with a large, immediate increase in Crashes (+73.99, p = .004). Critically, the effect of the 2023 revision was moderated by the number of fleeing Incidents; the policy's impact on Crashes was attenuated as Incidents increased (-0.070, p = .012). The findings were robust across all sensitivity analyses.

Conclusion: The restrictive 2020 policy was effective at immediately reducing crashes, but the 2023 revision reversed those gains. The moderating effect of Incidents on the 2023 policy's impact suggests a complex interplay between policy, enforcement activity, and outcomes. These findings provide critical, data-driven insights for law enforcement agencies on the real-world consequences of pursuit policy decisions.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of gender disparities on access to credit among female-led enterprises in Morocco, using firm-level data from the 2023 World Bank Enterprise Survey. Employing a quasi-experimental approach based on Propensity Score Matching (PSM), we compare credit access between firms managed or owned by women and those led exclusively by men. The findings reveal that gender inequalities do not constitute a major barrier to obtaining credit when the firm characteristics are comparable. On average, female-led firms are 9-13% more likely to secure a credit line than their male counterparts, depending on the matching method used. Factors such as firm size and geographic location exert a more significant influence on credit access than gender. These results challenge narratives emphasizing systematic gender discrimination in financial markets and suggest that broader structural factors must be addressed to enhance financial inclusion. Policy efforts aimed at expanding access to finance could serve as effective channels for promoting economic growth and fostering female entrepreneurship in Morocco.

title: Setting Higher Standards: How Governments Can Regulate Corporate Human Rights Performance
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: Setting Higher Standards: How Governments Can Regulate Corporate Human Rights Performance
detail.abstract:
In recent years, we have seen a wave of new regulatory frameworks, including legislation seeking to regulate businesses for their human rights impacts. 

Starting with voluntary initiatives like the UN’s Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and more recently with the European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), this report assesses the rise and key tenets of business and human rights regulation. It then provides recommendations to governments and companies on how to maximize the effectiveness of the legislation. Much of the regulatory activity has occurred in Europe, but this report argues for enhanced US government engagement. 

Central to our prescription is the idea that governments need to develop and enforce performance standards and metrics by which corporate compliance can be assessed and companies held accountable. Regulation is important, but without more data and means for assessing compliance and progress, regulation will not achieve its potential. Below is a summary of recommendations for governments and companies.

title: Achieving Hyper-Performance: The Role of Trust Calibration and Persuasive AI in Strategic Decision-Making
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Achieving Hyper-Performance: The Role of Trust Calibration and Persuasive AI in Strategic Decision-Making
detail.abstract: This study investigates the critical behavioral mechanisms underlying successful human-AI collaboration for achieving organizational hyper-performance a state of sustained superior agility, innovation, and adaptability. While AI offers immense computational power, its integration is hampered by a significant knowledge-behavior gap and prevalent algorithm aversion. Addressing this, we develop and test a novel theoretical framework, the Cognitive Synergy Loop, which integrates persuasive systems design with dynamic capabilities theory. Through a 2x2 between-subjects experiment (N = 210), we manipulate AI interface type (Standard Advisory vs. Cognitive-Synergy) and task complexity. Results indicate that the Cognitive-Synergy AI, designed to diagnose biases and deliver persuasive nudges, significantly enhances decision quality. This relationship is partially mediated by calibrated trust and is moderated by domain expertise, with stronger effects for experts. The findings provide robust evidence that designing AI to act as a collaborative coach, rather than an oracle, is key to unlocking hyper-performance, offering significant theoretical and practical contributions for the future of work.

title: Harmful Content: The Role of Internet Platform Companies in Fighting Terrorist Incitement and Politically Motivated Disinformation
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University, New York University (NYU) - New York University, New York University (NYU) - New York University and Independent

detail.title: Harmful Content: The Role of Internet Platform Companies in Fighting Terrorist Incitement and Politically Motivated Disinformation
detail.abstract:
The internet does a lot of good for the estimated 3.5 billion people who use it today. But increasingly, harmful content contaminates the web, threatening democratic institutions and human rights around the globe.

In this white paper, the World Economic Forum Global Future Council on Human Rights focuses on two types of dangerous online content: terrorist incitement and politically motivated disinformation. Though emanating from different sources, both seek to distort the truth, discredit liberal institutions, and, in the words of the European Parliament, undermine “democratic values, human rights, and the rule of law”. 

Internet companies have resisted government content regulations. They justifiably worry that many states would seek to suppress dissenting views, undermining free speech online. The danger in this regard is all too obvious. A number of governments have blocked Facebook, Twitter, and Google. 

In the absence of government regulation, however, it is incumbent on the major platforms to assume a more active self-governance role. Corporate leaders should take responsibility to vindicate core societal interests, such as combating political disinformation and terrorist incitement, while elevating journalistic reporting and civil discourse.

ISIS and other terrorist groups have exploited social media in an unprecedented manner to recruit new members and encourage violence. The group’s digital propaganda has helped motivate an army of foreign fighters (once estimated to be as large as 40,000) to take up its cause in Syria and Iraq, and has inspired a range of devastating attacks by self-directed supporters overseas. 

With regard to the 2016 presidential campaign, American intelligence agencies have concluded that Russian agents systematically spread false information online and in so doing, undermined "public faith in the democratic process". "Trolls" posing as Americans used Twitter to push messages larded with made-up news and conspiracy theories. Facebook has revealed that fake accounts operated by Russians bought thousands of online advertisements on divisive social and political issues.

title: Toward Responsible Mining: Linking ESG Strategies with Spatial Analysis in Zambia's Copper Mining Industry
affiliations: , University of Cambridge - Department of Engineering, Independent, University College London - Institute for Sustainable Resources, Univ. Grenoble Alpes,  ISTerre, Independent, Independent, University of Cambridge - Department of Engineering and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Toward Responsible Mining: Linking ESG Strategies with Spatial Analysis in Zambia's Copper Mining Industry
detail.abstract: Concerns over the environmental and social impacts of mining have prompted the development of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) frameworks to guide companies toward more sustainable practices. While these frameworks have enhanced accountability and encouraged responsible mining, questions remain about their effectiveness in addressing localised impacts. This study combines a comprehensive review of mining-related mitigation measures with a geospatial analysis of Zambia's copper mining sector, integrating multiple datasets to evaluate environmental risks and social vulnerabilities. A novel quantitative scoring method is employed to assess mitigation options, utilising geospatial data that includes demographic statistics and infrastructure indicators such as roads, buildings, and public services, to identify socioeconomic challenges associated with mining activities. The analysis reveals significant regional differences: older mines in the Copperbelt Province face greater environmental and social hazards compared to newer operations in the NorthWestern Province. Factors such as historical land use, river systems, and infrastructure investment contribute to these disparities. Notably, modern mining sites like Trident exhibit lower population pressures and improved infrastructure, suggesting that stronger ESG compliance can help mitigate localised impacts. By integrating ESG mitigation strategies with geospatial analysis, this study offers a robust framework for promoting sustainable mining practices, with broader applicability to other resource-rich regions facing similar challenges.

title: Towards a Low-Carbon West Kalimantan: Budget Tagging Strategy for Reducing GHG Emissions and Improving Environmental Impact Assessment (IKLH)

detail.title: Towards a Low-Carbon West Kalimantan: Budget Tagging Strategy for Reducing GHG Emissions and Improving Environmental Impact Assessment (IKLH)
detail.abstract: The West Kalimantan Provincial Government is targeting a 27.99% reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and an increase in the Environmental Quality Index (IKLH) to 73.21 by 2026. This target aligns with Indonesia's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) commitment as stipulated in Presidential Regulation No. 98/2021 concerning the Economic Value of Carbon. This study analyzes the effectiveness of budget tagging mechanisms for strategic programs and sub-activities in the agriculture, forestry, energy, and environmental sectors, involving the Regional Development Planning Agency (Bappeda), USAID SEGAR, and four locus districts (Sintang, Ketapang, Kubu Raya, and Sanggau). The results indicate that priority interventions include forest/land fire prevention, waste management, and monitoring of fertilizer and pesticide use. Budget tagging has been proven to strengthen synergy between provinces and facilitate data-based performance evaluation. This policy brief recommends integrating budget tagging into regional development planning documents and increasing local government capacity to optimize climate and sustainable development outcomes.

title: Spreading The Big Lie: How Social Media Sites Have Amplified False Claims of U.S. Election Fraud
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: Spreading The Big Lie: How Social Media Sites Have Amplified False Claims of U.S. Election Fraud
detail.abstract:
The claim that Joe Biden did not legitimately win the 2020 election has evolved from a backward-looking Big Lie to an article of faith in the Republican Party that elections in the United States are generally corrupt. GOP nominees for state and federal office have elevated the falsehood to a central campaign theme in the 2022 midterms. 

Social media platforms have promised to protect the upcoming elections from mis- and disinformation, but their flawed policies and inconsistent enforcement result in the continued amplification of election denialism, especially in key battleground states. 

The consequences of denialism are grave. Beyond undermining trust in elections and other democratic institutions, the phenomenon is used to justify enactment of restrictive voting laws that disproportionately harm people of color. Denialism has also fueled harassment and death threats aimed at election administrators, causing many experienced officials to make plans to leave their jobs before the 2024 presidential election, a prospect that would increase the chances of logistical snafus and reinforce baseless claims of fraud. 

If even a handful of Republican deniers are elected this year to state offices that oversee presidential elections—such as governor and secretary of state—the 2024 process could descend into chaos and violence, making the events of 2020 - 2021 seem tame by comparison. This report assesses the role the major social media platforms have Executive Summary played in the spread of election denialism and recommends what they can do now to mitigate further harm to democratic institutions and norms.

title: The AMH Fashion Company: Navigating the GCC and COVID-19 Crises

detail.abstract: In an ever-changing global landscape marked by unpredictable crises, businesses face monumental challenges in ensuring continuity and resilience. This case study explores the strategic crisis and risk management manoeuvres of a premier private fashion enterprise in Qatar, which has been disguised as AMH. Anchored in the tumultuous experiences of the 2017 GCC crisis and the global upheaval caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, this narrative unfolds the tactics behind AMH's ability to not only survive but also navigate through these formidable periods. Furthermore, each crisis brings up various lessons to learn for the future, and the management needs to absorb these lessons and implement them in the future. It examines its crisis and risk management strategies along with the leadership skills shown during the 2017 GCC crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic. The case puts forward the measures taken by the firm to overcome the challenges by implementing effective strategies. By exploring how AMH's leadership harnessed the storms of geopolitical discord and a health catastrophe, this case study offers a compelling look into the importance of preparedness, agility, and the invaluable lessons drawn from the heart of crises that define the future trajectories of businesses worldwide.

title: The Axiom Engine: A Fractal Framework for Anti-Fragile Governance and AI Alignment

detail.title: The Axiom Engine: A Fractal Framework for Anti-Fragile Governance and AI Alignment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no competing financial interests. The author does declare a non-financial competing interest in that they are the architect of the theoretical framework presented in this paper and therefore have a strong pre-existing intellectual commitment to its validity and efficacy.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article does not contain any studies involving human participants or animals performed by the author.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Axiom Engine, a novel philosophical and operational framework designed to address systemic decay in complex societies. The framework posits that by institutionalizing a fractal, self-correcting architecture based on the core pillars of Truth, Wisdom, and Humanity, systems from the individual to the global level can achieve anti-fragility—the capacity to gain strength from disorder. We first detail the philosophical architecture, which models ethical space as a tetrahedral field. We then describe its operational engine, a synthesis of cybernetic feedback loops and second-order observation. Subsequently, we demonstrate the framework's fractal scalability through proposed redesigns of personal ethics, the U.S. Constitution, the UN Charter, and a solution for the AI alignment problem. The paper argues that the Axiom Engine offers a coherent, scalable, and robust alternative to static governance models, providing a generative protocol for navigating 21st-century complexity.

title: False Accusation: The Unfounded Claim that Social Media Companies Censor Conservatives
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University and New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: False Accusation: The Unfounded Claim that Social Media Companies Censor Conservatives
detail.abstract:
Conservatives commonly accuse the major social media companies of censoring the political right. In response to Twitter’s decision on January 8, 2021, to exclude him from the platform, then-President Donald Trump accused the company of “banning free speech” in coordination with “the Democrats and Radical Left.”

Two days earlier, Trump had included the ideological bias claim in an incendiary address to supporters, some of whom then participated in a riot inside the U.S. Capitol. “The radical left tries to blacklist you on social media,” Trump said in his speech. “They don’t let the message get out nearly as they should.” 

This accusation—that social media platforms suppress conservatives— riles a Republican base that has long distrusted the mainstream media and is prone to seeing public events as being shaped by murky liberal plots. On a policy level, the bias claim serves as a basis for Republican attacks on Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, the federal law that protects platforms from liability associated with user posts and content moderation decisions. 

But the claim of anti-conservative animus is itself a form of disinformation: a falsehood with no reliable evidence to support it. No trustworthy large-scale studies have determined that conservative content is being removed for ideological reasons or that searches are being manipulated to favor liberal interests. 

Even anecdotal evidence of supposed bias tends to crumble under close examination. Take Trump’s exclusion from Twitter and Facebook. These actions, while unprecedented, were reasonable responses to Trump’s repeated violation of platform rules against undermining election results and inciting violence. If anything, the platforms previously had given Trump a notably wide berth because of his position, seeking to appease him, despite his demagogic and routinely false claims. 

Trump has been the leading purveyor of the bias accusation, but it will not recede with the end of his presidency. In his quest to remain politically relevant, Trump almost certainly will continue to press the case via far-right media channels and/or right-wing online platforms like Parler and Gab. After getting kicked off Twitter, Trump said he might set up a platform of his own. Other Republican politicians likewise will maintain the accusation, in no small part because it resonates so powerfully with so many GOP voters.
